why_angle: The cited rivals each print half of the picture. Charge-Test gives XTAR's measured energy and Light And Matter gives EBL's, but neither sets measured energy next to the label. So nobody shows that the 38% label lead the XTAR 4150 has over the EBL 3000 shrinks to 0.5–4.5% when measured, that the EBL beats its own label while the XTARs reach 82–86% of theirs, or that the label that looks biggest (PUJIMAX 4,255 mWh) measured the least. The page also adds Gough Lui's mAh × voltage check, which explains the gap, and his cycle-wear test, which Charge-Test says it did not do.

page.title: Best Rechargeable Lithium AA Batteries (1.5V): Measured Energy vs the Label
page.h1: Best rechargeable lithium batteries: what 1.5V AA cells really hold
page.desc: Measured energy for XTAR CLR 4300, XTAR 4150, K&F Concept and EBL 1.5V lithium AA batteries, shown against each label, with charger fit and cost per measured Wh.
page.answer: Short answer. The best rechargeable lithium AA batteries are the XTAR CLR 4300. In a 20-model 1.5V lab test it delivered 3,703 mWh, the most of any model, though that is only 86% of its 4,300 mWh label. EBL's 3000 mWh cells beat their own label, so compare tested energy, not the label.

cells.lowbatt: Voltage slopes down to about 1.0 V, so a battery gauge can warn you (XTAR)
cells.charger: XTAR L4 Pro, MX4, L4, L8 or VX4 V2 (not VX4 V1)

cells.lowbatt: Steps down to 1.1 V for about the last 20% of runtime (Gough Lui)
cells.charger: XTAR 1.5V Li-ion charger (Gough Lui tested it on the XTAR L4)

cells.measured: 3,273–3,404 mWh, 8 cells on an XTAR VX4 V2 (Light And Matter)
cells.lowbatt: The gauge reads full until the cells are dead, then drops to empty at once (Light And Matter)
cells.charger: A 1.5V Li-ion charger; a NiMH charger won't charge them (Light And Matter)

page.after:
What the differences mean

  • Label versus measured. CLR 4300: 3,703 ÷ 4,300 = 86%. XTAR 4150: 3,420 ÷ 4,150 = 82%. K&F: 3,278 ÷ 3,600 = 91%. EBL: 3,273–3,404 ÷ 3,000 = 109–113%.
  • The 38% lead on the label nearly disappears. By label, the XTAR 4150 holds 38% more than the EBL (4,150 ÷ 3,000 = 1.38). Measured, the lead is 0.5–4.5% (3,420 ÷ 3,404 = 1.005; 3,420 ÷ 3,273 = 1.045). The two figures come from different test rigs, so treat this as a direction, not a head-to-head result.
  • CLR 4300 against the XTAR 4150. 3,703 ÷ 3,420 = 1.083, so the CLR 4300 gives 8% more energy per charge. At 1 A the gap grows to 13% (3,719 ÷ 3,297).
  • Cost per measured Wh at maker-store prices on 10 Nov 2026. CLR 4300: 26.99 ÷ (4 × 3.703 Wh) = 1.82 dollars per Wh. K&F, charger included: 24.99 ÷ (8 × 3.278 Wh) = 0.95 dollars per Wh. EBL: 31.48 ÷ (4 × 3.273–3.404 Wh) = 2.31–2.40 dollars per Wh.

Why the label on a 1.5V lithium AA overstates it

A 1.5V lithium AA is a 3.6V Li-ion cell with a converter that holds the output near 1.5V (XTAR). The mWh printed on the label is not what reaches your device. The XTAR 4150 shows how this works. 4,150 mWh ÷ 1.5 V would be 2,767 mAh, yet XTAR rates the cell at only 2,500 mAh. Gough Lui measured 2,422 mAh at 0.5 A, at an average of 1.42 V: 2,422 × 1.42 = 3,439 mWh. That agrees with Charge-Test's separate 3,420 mWh. The mAh rating was close to the truth; the mWh rating was the one inflated. The EBL runs the other way: it carries no mAh rating, and Light And Matter measured more energy than its 3,000 mWh label.

Current matters too. On XTAR's own test-results page, Gough Lui's CLR 4300 cells gave 2,599–2,739 mAh at 1 A but only 2,298–2,438 mAh at 2 A. For the XTAR 4150, Gough Lui advises staying under 1.25 A.

Lifespan is the other number missing from the label. Charge-Test says its ranking does not cover service life. Gough Lui ran the XTAR 4150 through 100 cycles in the lab and measured a loss of 0.85–0.89 mWh per cycle. That projects to 80% of its energy at about 843 cycles, against XTAR's 1,200-cycle rating (843 ÷ 1,200 = 70%). XTAR supplied the samples. Of the cells on this page, the 4150 is the only one with a published cycle-wear test, which makes it the pick if you want measured durability as well as near-top energy: {buy:xtar-1-5v-aa-4150mwh-8-pack}.

Charging is the catch. The cells manage their own charging and need a charger that supplies 4.75–5.5 V. A NiMH-only charger won't work, and XTAR says its older VX4 V1 cannot charge the CLR 4300. The XTAR L4 Pro (15.90 dollars at XTAR on 10 Nov 2026) charges both 1.5V Li-ion and NiMH AA/AAA cells.

Not recommended

PUJIMAX AA (4,255 mWh label). It has the biggest number on the shelf and delivered about 2,255 mWh in Charge-Test's lab, 53% of its label (2,255 ÷ 4,255). The Hixon 3500 (3,339 mWh) and UseNiy 3600 (3,162 mWh) also tested below both XTAR cells. EBL for Apple mice and keyboards, or flashes: an EBL store listing says its 1.5V lithium AAs can't be used in Apple mice and keyboards, and Light And Matter measured flash recycle times up to 8 times slower than NiMH.
